mcqs.question: Why does using an if instead of a while to guard a wait() call create a bug?
options: Because wait() can return due to a spurious wakeup with no matching notify(), and an if guard doesn't re-check the condition afterward
Because if statements execute slower than while loops under contention
Because notify() can only be called once per object during its lifetime
Because wait() requires the guard to be a while loop by Java language syntax rules
mcqs.explanation: The JVM spec permits spurious wakeups — wait() returning with no matching notify() — so an if guard that never re-checks the condition can proceed on a stale assumption. There's no such speed difference, notify() has no one-time-use limit, and Java's syntax accepts an if guard just as validly; the bug is logical, not syntactic.

mcqs.question: Why might a producer be unable to simply block when the queue is full?
options: Blocking queues do not support producer threads at all
A request-handling thread blocking on a full queue ties up a thread-pool slot, which can cascade into unrelated timeouts elsewhere
Because blocking always causes a deadlock within one second
Because Java forbids calling put() from more than one producer thread
mcqs.explanation: A blocked request-handling thread stops serving other requests, and if enough threads block, the whole pool can starve, cascading into timeouts unrelated to this specific queue. BlockingQueue fully supports producer threads, blocking doesn't inherently cause deadlock, and multiple producers calling put() concurrently is explicitly supported.

mcqs.question: Why is switching to an unbounded queue not a real fix for backpressure?
options: Unbounded queues are not supported by any standard Java collection
It relocates the risk from a blocked producer to unbounded memory growth, risking an eventual out-of-memory crash if consumers fall behind
Unbounded queues silently drop items once a queue reaches capacity
It requires rewriting every consumer to run in a single thread
mcqs.explanation: An unbounded queue trades a visible, recoverable blocking problem for an invisible one — unconstrained growth that eventually exhausts memory. Java's LinkedBlockingQueue supports an unbounded mode directly, it never silently drops items, and consumer threading is unaffected by queue boundedness.
